lines: Picture a few hundred cities, and every single pair of them wants its fastest route, all at once.
One way: a single dynamic program that checks every possible waypoint, for every pair, together.
Another way: the single-source algorithm, already built, run once from every city in turn.
One of these approaches has a fixed cost — it never cares how many roads actually exist, only how many cities.
The other's cost grows with the number of roads.
On a huge map with comparatively few roads between cities, which one does less total work?
answer: The one whose cost is tied to the roads, not the cities.
The fixed-cost approach does the identical amount of work no matter how sparse the map is. The other one's cost shrinks right along with the road count — so on a sparse map, it comes out ahead.

lines: Here's the dynamic program's own mechanism. It fills a whole table of distances, one allowed waypoint at a time.
For every single pair of cities, it asks one question: does routing through this new waypoint beat the best route found so far?
Repeat that question for every waypoint, and the whole table ends up correct.
A distance alone can't tell you which road actually got taken — two completely different routes can add up to the exact same number.
So keep a second table alongside the first. Each cell remembers one thing: the city visited right before the destination.
Follow that, one step backward at a time, and the actual route falls right out.
Take that identical table-filling idea, and strip out the numbers entirely.
Instead of adding distances, just ask whether both halves of a route are already reachable.
Same waypoints, same order, same rule for updating a cell — now it answers which city can reach which.
Add one new city to the map, connected to every other city by a free road.
Run the slower, more general algorithm once from that new city, and use what it finds to adjust every single road's own length.
Could that adjustment ever flip which route between two cities is the cheapest one?
answer: No. Every route between the same two cities shifts by the identical amount.

Whichever route you take between two fixed cities, the adjustment adds up to the exact same total. Shifting every option in a comparison by the same amount can never change which one was smallest to begin with.

lines: Every algorithm in this chapter, so far, has answered a question about two cities, or one city against all the rest.
Neither of today's two answers needed a new trick underneath — just a new way of putting the old ones together.
The next kind of map has no loops in it at all, and that changes everything about how cheap the answer gets.
